sections.heading: A comprehensive academic renderer, made convenient
paragraphs: RadianceLab aims to make an academic renderer as comprehensive and convenient as possible. The ambition has three dimensions: bring established transport families into one application, support a broad range of image-formation models, and make the scene easy to author and inspect. Breadth is useful when an experiment can move from an idea to a visible result without rebuilding its surrounding tools.

The C++ and OpenGL application puts ten modes behind a common scene and camera workflow. Familiar camera and light tracing sit beside bidirectional connection, photon gathering, Metropolis mutation and path guiding. RGB/spectral operation, material and emission models, participating media and optical instruments extend the kinds of experiment that can be expressed. The implementation table identifies the supported and experimental parts of each route.

The application is also a visual working environment: move through the scene, edit a material graph, inspect an intermediate result, choose a lens and frame the image. Interactive feedback is the organizing goal; the selected producer, resolution and work budget determine how quickly a particular film refreshes or converges.

sections.heading: Original research inside the renderer: the photon hourglass
paragraphs: The research contribution extends this broad renderer by changing the representation of a transport sample. Hand-pick which coordinates of a path to sweep, and the photon-primitive framework turns that choice into a technique: sweeping nothing leaves a photon point, and the swept coordinates otherwise form a beam, ring, arc, surface or volume; a camera ray queries that support, and its density and change of measure carry into a contribution weighted under MIS against the other techniques. RadianceLab brings these families together in the most complete implementation of the photon-primitive framework I am aware of. This is a claim about coverage of that framework, not about being a more complete renderer in general.

The hourglass construction is the central example. A sampled source and a spherical dielectric define refracted rays that rotate around a symmetry axis. Their sweep forms a ruled sheet. Analytic crossings recover the contribution of a camera ray without spreading it over a finite beam radius; vertex-seeded variants and compatible partners explore different ways to sample the same difficult structure.

The core path contains two specular transmissions followed by one volume-scattering event. Extensions add eligible specular chains, reflections, and camera-side specular paths. The hourglass handles these multi-interface caustics and joins other strategies in one combined estimator. Each transport contribution is counted once: overlapping strategies can be combined with MIS, while independently added estimators must cover disjoint path classes. Otherwise, for example, a beam and a plane could both count the same double-scattered light.

sections.heading: Make the sampling structure visible
paragraphs: The renderer exposes the work behind the viewfinder: sampled paths, photon clouds and trees, connection and merge events, mutation activity, guiding directions and swept-primitive crossings. In the photon-primitive research, correlated modes reuse a shared pool so neighboring pixels reveal the same geometric objects. Freezing that pool turns a noisy film into an inspectable arrangement of contributions.

Sharing samples changes spatial covariance; it does not automatically lower variance or accelerate every estimator. Normalization uses the number of primitives drawn, including those that miss. The project keeps this distinction explicit while testing primitive reuse, finite-radius estimators, and mixtures on compatible path measures.

sections.heading: From live scene work to a finished image
paragraphs: The workflow begins in the rendered scene. Pick an object, author its material or medium through typed nodes, inspect previews and apply the edit. Navigate in first person, change light placement, adjust a finite aperture or use dolly zoom to alter perspective while retaining a subject’s framing. An imported image or clean-frame capture can be projected onto a surface and baked into UV coordinates.

Hold the camera to refine the progressive film, then use tone mapping and the image-processing tools to shape its presentation. Comparison reports preserve displayed images and scene settings; the photon-primitive research also has floating-point film exports for numerical analysis. Viewfinder responsiveness and final convergence remain separate measurements, because the GPU, hybrid and CPU producers perform different work per pass.

Research results are evaluated within their stated model and path support. The original notes retain finite-difference Jacobians, limiting cases, same-draw comparisons and convergence studies. That evidence supports the hourglass and related primitive developments while keeping the surrounding renderer useful for broader material, lighting and imaging exploration.

sections.heading: From a 3D-to-Rive idea to a graphics laboratory
paragraphs: My first idea was to turn a real-time 3D render into a .riv animation. A Rive scripting competition entry explored that direction with a small hybrid rasterizer and ray tracer. Moving into C++ gave me room to ask what should become geometry and animation keys, what should remain an image, and what might be reconstructed as NPR contours.

A parallel route lets .riv supply animation and interaction while a GPU host renders the world. Discovering GPU Canvas made that connection especially interesting: I tried both delivery formats, then used the host for compute-based experiments beyond the current GPU Canvas shader API.

Implementing Rive’s drawing interface led to custom curves and soft fields. A small editor and content-aware effect stack made those experiments usable; a photon-mapping and time-of-flight renderer supplied richer scenes to export. The brochure follows that progression, showing the result of each choice and its limits.

sections.heading: Choose what the player needs to keep
paragraphs: A standalone .riv contains the supported shapes, assets and animation needed by an official Rive runtime. Keyed animation and vector-compatible effect output use this route. In a browser bundle, Rive animation can instead drive a WebGL renderer, or Rive layers can share the view with a GPU-rendered field. The bundle includes the host code that coordinates those pieces.

The official-Rive world-path replay projects retained 3D paths into reusable Rive shapes, with live camera and time-gate controls. The custom RIVX3D viewer draws retained samples directly in WebGL2. The desktop studio keeps the full scene and graph editable; each export preserves the behavior it was designed to carry. Separate signed GPU Canvas studies package their own authored GPU behavior in Rive. The desktop exporter does not yet convert an arbitrary scene or effect stack into that form.

sections.heading: Two backends, the same animation
paragraphs: The studio uses the official open-source Rive renderer and a custom backend implementing the Rive renderer and factory interfaces. Switching between them makes it possible to compare the same asset while developing new effects and representations.

The RIVX backend exposes object identity, depth, motion and contours, together with HDR targets and specialized primitives. A stack can combine geometry-aware treatments with raster passes; vector-producing stages can feed Rive output. The official backend remains the reference for supported Rive playback, while custom curves, splats and auxiliary-field effects extend the native workflow.

sections.heading: Edit the shape, extend the primitive
paragraphs: A small editor supports shape and curve adjustments alongside playback. Extended primitives include interpolating Yuksel curves, B-splines and anisotropic 2D Gaussian splats. Keeping their native representation lets the renderer preserve information that an ordinary cubic path or round feather would approximate.

Export offers a practical choice: preserve the extension in RIVX, flatten an extended curve for portable .riv, or approximate a splat with supported vector shapes and feathering. The recordings show the original and the chosen representation, so the visual tradeoff is visible.

sections.heading: Animate light, then decide how to draw it
paragraphs: The 3D workspace combines rasterized geometry with path tracing, photon mapping and baked surface lighting. Time-of-flight studies keep light-arrival times so an animated gate can reveal propagation through the scene.

Points, beams and rings make transport directly drawable. Surface lightmaps provide a dense appearance; contours, hatches and isocurves turn selected fields into vector structure. Deeper baking can replace a lighting texture with an approximate family of curves, which makes the representation itself part of the experiment.

This connects to RadianceLab through photon-primitive geometry, with a different delivery question: how can the result become an animated drawing that a smaller player can reproduce? A fixed animation can bake its appearance into keys, while a retained-path viewer can keep camera and time-gate interaction over the exported cache.

sections.heading: From an editable scene to a playable asset
paragraphs: Use ordinary .riv for supported vector effects and authored animation. The keyed route reuses compatible geometry, images and properties across frames; deeper vector baking approximates fields with isocurves or hatch paths. These are choices about which representation best preserves the intended appearance.

For more live behavior, export a Rive-driven WebGL bundle, a hybrid composition of Rive layers and a GPU canvas, or retained world paths drawn by official Rive. A browser bundle carries the viewer code with the asset; it is a different deliverable from a standalone .riv.

Keep the native RIVX project when the work still needs its editable graph, extended primitives or fresh scene evaluation. Shader effects, Yuksel/B-spline geometry and exact splat fields may need that enhanced renderer or an approximation for portable playback.

limitations: Export depends on the effect: vector-compatible results can become .riv; richer shader and auxiliary-buffer effects use a raster bake, hybrid viewer or the enhanced RIVX backend.
Keyed .riv preserves an authored animation. New camera views, refraction or lighting changes need the corresponding retained data or fresh computation; baked images retain their source resolution.

Signed GPU Canvas studies have their own authored GPU behavior. General desktop scene/effect-stack conversion to that form is not yet available; other browser exports preserve their selected workflow.
The official-Rive world-path replay uses 384 shapes and four display colors over a fixed cache. It is a transport-structure visualization; it does not recompute visibility or scattering weights.
The backends have different feature coverage and costs. Native timings and export checks are available; controlled mobile/browser and equal-error transport comparisons remain open.

title: Modal2D
kicker: Draw a shape, solve its modes, tune it into an instrument, then play a score with a choir of them.
summary: Create a fully physically based virtual musical instrument, starting with a shape, its mass and stiffness. sections.heading: Play a manually tuned instrument, then try creating your own
paragraphs: The manually tuned instrument mode provides designed families with playable note regions. The instrument creation lab takes the more open-ended route: start from a shape, inspect how it vibrates, then search for geometry and contact choices that make it musical. These are two ways into the same physical model, with arbitrary-shape design as the lab's motivating question.

An instrument's geometry determines how it can vibrate, but its audible character also depends on where it is excited, which modes radiate, and how those modes decay. Modal2D makes that chain inspectable: build an object, solve its modes, strike or drive it, study the surrounding field, then alter its geometry to reach a target pitch.

Music mode brings the resulting designs together in a performance. A library of tuned shapes becomes an instrument set for typed scores and imported MIDI, with saved material and strike settings. The same geometric model is therefore used for numerical inspection, tuning and performance.

sections.heading: 01 · Geometry and material become a vibration model
paragraphs: Element stiffness and mass contributions assemble into sparse matrices K and M. The linear undamped modes satisfy Kφ = λMφ: φ is a spatial deformation pattern and λ = ω² gives frequency ω/(2π). Supports, material properties and geometry enter the model before sound is synthesized.

The implementation extends beyond its original in-plane meshes to mixed beams, thin and thick plate bending, shallow shells and an experimental tetrahedral-solid branch. Each formulation has its own degrees of freedom. Per-element materials, orthotropic triangles and explicit displacement-layout handling make these structural differences part of the computation.

sections.heading: 02 · Resolve and inspect the resonant basis
paragraphs: A custom generalized shift-invert Lanczos solver uses Eigen sparse factorization, mass-inner-product normalization and reorthogonalization to extract low modes. Small systems first try a single-precision dense cuSOLVER solve; systems above 512 degrees of freedom, or failed dense solves, use the sparse double-precision path.

Disconnected objects can acquire numerically mixed modes when their frequencies are close. Component-wise solves preserve localized modes when cavity coupling is disabled. The viewer makes the result inspectable through mode shapes, modal amplitudes, spectra and structural diagnostics; the mathematical basis is visible before it becomes a sound.

sections.heading: 03 · Excitation selects what becomes audible
paragraphs: A strike projects into the modal basis. Its location and direction determine which modes are excited, so striking a node and an antinode can produce different spectra from the same object. Repeated strikes add independent decaying events rather than restarting an existing ring.

The linear audio path sums damped modal oscillations with excitation and radiation weights. CUDA computes samples from persistent arrays of modal state and strike events, then returns PCM blocks to the host. Strike maps, spectra and audible playback connect the spatial explanation to the actual signal.

Continuous bowing solves a regularized friction force against the object’s modal surface velocity; pressure and bow speed change the sustained excitation. Rubbing uses a separate noise-driven contact, and the older repeated-impact bow remains available. The implicit friction solve uses a fixed iteration budget and a work limiter, so it is still a reduced contact model rather than a complete bow–string–instrument simulation.

A violin-like instrument shows why individually working features do not automatically make the final timbre. Its recognizable response depends on stable nonlinear stick–slip motion at the bow, a tensioned string, impedance transfer through the bridge, anisotropic curved plates, enclosed-air modes and radiation. Bow position, pressure and speed select the excitation; geometry, material, coupling and damping shape the dense body spectrum. Modal2D can bow a structure and add resonant-cavity response, but matching that complete feedback chain closely enough to sound like a violin remains an open construction problem.

sections.heading: 04 · Separate radiation from enclosed-air resonance
paragraphs: The surrounding-field display derives phase, envelope and other views from a dominant-frequency boundary-source phasor field. This is a useful visual model of interference and directional radiation. It is distinct from the enclosed-air path, which detects cavities, constructs acoustic meshes, solves cavity modes and couples them to a reduced structural basis.

The cavity display can show pressure beside structural vibration. Its current interface uses nearby structural displacement magnitude as a coupling proxy, and ports use a sealed-boundary approximation. The exterior display and optional cross-object feedback are also approximations; the project presents these as different levels of acoustic modeling rather than one universal sound-propagation solver.

sections.heading: 05 · Instrument creation lab: what if the shape came first?
paragraphs: Inverse tuning repeatedly changes geometry, rebuilds the model and measures pitch error in cents. Width/height searches, a finite-difference gradient option and a Bayesian search provide different ways to spend the solve budget. Mode tracking and excitation-based objectives address an important ambiguity: the lowest frequency, the tracked mode and the loudest excited mode need not be the same target.

For a musical range, the system first fits a size–frequency scaling law from two actual solves. That prediction initializes the existing Fine-W tuner; a new solve and refinement determine the saved result. Calibration, clamping and mode changes remain visible instead of turning the scaling formula into an assumed answer.

sections.heading: 06 · Assemble, save and perform the instrument set
paragraphs: Music mode schedules notes onto discovered instruments, rebuilds their saved geometry and preserves the associated materials and strike positions. MIDI import supplies notes, timing, velocity and selectable parts; it shares the typed-score playback and WAV-export path. Saved ensemble files retain both the score and the instrument setup.

Exact tuned-note matches are preferred. When a note is borrowed from a nearby instrument, the system explicitly scales that instrument's entire modal spectrum within a shift limit. This is pitch transposition of an existing modal instrument, not a claim that every MIDI pitch has a separately solved physical shape. The resulting performance is the final demonstration of the geometry-to-sound workflow.

limitations: Linear modal models approximate small vibration; nonlinear glide/shimmer and reverb are separate DSP effects, not nonlinear structural FEM. The tetrahedral-solid branch uses uniform radiation weighting.

Cavity coupling uses a node-lumped displacement-magnitude interface proxy, and ports use sealed boundaries. The exterior field is a monochromatic visualization; cross-object medium feedback is a heuristic rather than a coupled acoustic PDE solve.
The sparse eigensolver has a fixed Krylov-subspace pass rather than a verified thick-restart loop. Accuracy and tuning depend on discretization, retained modes and the objective being tracked.

MIDI import is a note/tempo reader, not a complete synthesizer or sequencer implementation. Nearby-note fallback transposes a solved spectrum rather than redesigning geometry. Automatic physical tuning remains the largest design limitation: the most reliable workflow is still a constrained one-parameter search plus manual refinement. Bracketed binary search works only while the chosen audible mode follows a suitable branch; mode switches and nonmonotonic pitch can defeat it.
CUDA synthesis synchronizes per audio block. Native performances and working sessions are recorded here; formal latency measurements and comparative validation remain separate work.

A convincing violin-like instrument remains open. Bow excitation and resonant-cavity response work, but the current system does not yet resolve the full nonlinear bow–string–bridge–curved-body–air feedback chain whose impedance, damping and mode coupling create the characteristic sound.

sections.heading: The interesting behavior happens between solvers
paragraphs: A material simulation becomes more revealing when its systems interact. Water should change the object it hits; heat should change how a solid deforms; a burning enclosure should respond to its oxygen supply. Crucible2.5D investigates these connections in an editable world, using different numerical representations for the quantities each handles well.

Crucible2.5D began as a 2D testbed for the advanced simulation techniques I wanted to explore. A planar world makes local interventions and internal fields easier to inspect, while leaving more of the interactive performance budget for coupled solvers, material history and experiments. The 2.5D name reflects selected thickness and support approximations added to these planar mechanics. Particle counts, grid resolution, field iterations and stiffness-dependent substeps still set practical limits.

The strongest demonstrations are causal experiments: switch a coupling or constitutive model, repeat the intervention, and inspect the difference. A grain-directed tear, a water jet striking a sand pile, and a chamber that exhausts its oxygen reveal more about the implementation than a large menu of isolated effects.

sections.heading: Three representations, explicit exchanges
paragraphs: SPH evaluates fluid density, pressure, viscosity and surface forces through particle neighborhoods. MPM transfers particle mass, momentum and constitutive stress onto a grid, updates the grid, and transfers motion back to the particles. A separate Eulerian solver advects air velocity and scalar fields and applies pressure projection. Signed-distance geometry supplies shared collision boundaries.

The exchanges are implemented as distinct GPU passes. The newer SPH–MPM contact path records reaction impulses and scatters them to a persistent grid for the following MPM step. Contact heat uses weighted thermal mixtures rather than retaining only the hottest neighbor. These are concrete improvements to coupling behavior; they do not make every subsystem an exactly conservative, monolithic solve.

sections.heading: Material direction becomes a failure mechanism
paragraphs: The MPM constitutive path includes elastic response, plasticity, temperature-dependent changes and fiber directions. Its anisotropic continuum-damage option adds a structural tensor, a monotone damage-driving history and a spatial damage Laplacian. Damage therefore depends on the material's direction and neighboring state, rather than only an isolated stretch threshold.

The Aniso Tear Bench provides a useful comparison between legacy fracture, isotropic damage and anisotropic damage. The implementation also exposes regularization length, residual stiffness and rate controls. This is a numerical material study: grid resolution, substeps and authored material parameters still affect the result.

sections.heading: Heat changes both motion and material state
paragraphs: Temperature diffusion and contact exchange feed material-specific phase, cure, gas and damage states. The baking and kiln experiments use different set temperatures, expansion rules and stiffness changes, making the same heating process produce different outcomes. These authored constitutive models are exploratory material behavior, not calibrated predictions for food or industrial processing.

Combustion has an oxygen field and fuel-vapor state, supporting starvation, smoldering and backdraft experiments. Explosions add an analytic expanding front using a two-dimensional Sedov-style radius law with an acoustic-speed transition. Separate passes deposit heat, flow sources and particle impulses as the front crosses the scene; this makes arrival and interaction visible without claiming a full compressible shock solver.

sections.heading: Fields become material behavior
paragraphs: The magnetic path combines an analytic external pole field with per-particle magnetization and an optional grid-based self-field. It supports experiments in attraction, repulsion, thermal response and remanence. Ferrofluid surface spikes also use an explicit surface-traction model and seeded corrugation, so their appearance is presented as a controlled approximation rather than evidence of a validated instability calculation.

The magnetic-lift recording contrasts field-driven shaping with a mechanical Spring Drag tool in the same pool. The field raises a narrow column and neighboring peaks; the drag moves a selected patch directly. These planar peaks have different curvature and connectivity from three-dimensional ferrofluid spikes.

Living-material experiments connect continuous cellular automata and reaction–diffusion fields to deformable particles. SmoothLife, Lenia and Gray–Scott variants drive field patterns; membrane forces, vitality and particle insertion translate those patterns into motion and growth. The distinction is deliberate: this is artificial-life behavior coupled to mechanics, not a biological tissue model.

sections.heading: Expose the cause alongside the appearance
paragraphs: The scene browser, feature tour and pipeline diagrams organize the implementation into experiments. Temperature, material-state and driving-field views make hidden quantities inspectable, while surface, particle and luminous rendering styles show how the same state can be presented differently.

A focused presentation pairs each result with one diagnostic: damage and fiber direction for fracture; temperature and oxygen for fire; the field beneath a ferrofluid surface; or the continuous automaton beneath a growing material. The portfolio emphasizes these mechanisms and comparisons, with artistic rendering kept distinct from simulation evidence.

limitations: A real-time experimental sandbox with authored constitutive responses, stabilization and optional artistic forces; it is not a calibrated engineering or biological simulator.

Dimensionality changes the mechanics: pores that cross a narrow 2D ligament can sever its load path, while a 3D porous solid may retain connections around the opening through depth. Thickness and support heuristics approximate selected missing behavior; they do not recover full 3D topology.
Damage regularization is currently parameterized relative to grid spacing, and elastic substeps are capped. Resolution independence and unrestricted numerical stability are not established.
SPH–MPM reaction exchange is staged across steps. The entire coupled world is not claimed to conserve energy or momentum exactly.
Magnetic spikes and explosion fronts include explicit approximations. Rendered depth, glow and surface detail do not imply a full three-dimensional simulation.
The recordings demonstrate selected material responses and interactions. Broader numerical convergence and calibration against real materials remain open work.

sections.heading: A playground for shader systems
paragraphs: Running a Shadertoy-style shader locally is the starting point. The more interesting problem appears when the result depends on multiple buffers, retained history or several interacting simulations: the program is a network, and its topology affects the result.

ShaderWeave makes that network explicit. Source editors, channel connections and live image nodes form one workspace. A visitor can follow an intermediate texture into a downstream transformation or a feedback loop, then see which part of the computation changed when the shader was edited.

The editor, graph and execution system are my work. Several shader artworks in the recordings are imported examples by other creators, including Inigo Quilez’s Snail; the brochure credits their original authors and works.

sections.heading: Use topology to construct behavior
paragraphs: The included examples go beyond a chain of post effects. A rolling volume writes one source frame into a slice of a persistent 3D texture; a viewer unwraps that ring into a recent-time volume. The image becomes a spatial record of a temporal process.

A diffusion/fusion example separates diffusion, fusion and reaction into connected passes. Persistent ping-pong storage gives feedback an explicit temporal boundary. This distinction matters: reading a previous frame is a state update, whereas an unresolved same-frame dependency cycle has no valid evaluation order. The graph makes both the useful structure and its execution constraints inspectable.

sections.heading: A framebuffer is a useful interface boundary
paragraphs: GLSL raster and compute paths, CUDA compilation and OptiX rendering provide different ways to produce an image. Their output textures can participate in the surrounding shader workflow. This lets a ray-traced or computed result become material for further experiments instead of an isolated application window.

The boundary is deliberately concrete: texture output and channel binding. CUDA and OptiX retain their own compilation, launch and resource requirements; supporting their output does not make them interchangeable with an ordinary fragment pass. The system is a Windows desktop playground with NVIDIA-dependent paths, rather than a portable browser graph runtime.

sections.heading: Keep the computation visible while it changes
paragraphs: Inline previews are the main interface contribution. They let a procedural field, accumulated history and final composite remain visible together, so debugging becomes a comparison between stages. Node styling can itself use shader output, making the tool an additional surface for its own experiments.

Preview scheduling is also a systems problem: a shared dependency should not be recomputed for every visible consumer, and retained buffers must advance consistently. The included versions contain different preview paths. A shared render plan supports reuse, but the total cost of previews and repeated dependencies still needs runtime measurement.

evolution.heading: Authorship and evolution
paragraphs: I wrote ShaderWeave almost entirely by hand, with AI used during later polishing phases. The original project established the live node-and-buffer workflow; the newer source explores a revised graph interface and execution paths.

The earlier showcase remains available with its original screenshots. Those captures document the existing project history; a new recording should show the current feedback and preview behavior before claiming a performance improvement.

limitations: Shadertoy-style inputs and multipass workflows are supported; some shaders or features still require adaptation.
The active application includes a network snapshot exporter and saved .lfnet.json examples. A complete import/export round trip remains unverified.
Source inspection confirms a cached active-component render plan. Its total preview and GPU cost still needs a focused runtime benchmark.

sections.heading: Watch topology and behavior evolve
paragraphs: I wanted to understand learning through physical tasks I could watch and interact with. Building the machinery from the ground up lets me follow the whole loop: what a controller senses, how its network responds and how training changes its behavior. The workbench makes established learning methods tangible through their moving parts.

The main route is neuroevolution: NEAT changes network connections and weights while a curriculum raises gravity and widens starting angles. CMA-ES searches a fixed architecture; PPO supplies a genuine actor–critic backpropagation route. A compact ready-to-play menu groups controllers by task and colors their technique. Pendulum entries combine their recorded release with a hold-and-nudge toggle, while a separate selector starts fresh training.

A frozen generation-120 NEAT policy recovered and finished upright in all 40 unseen near-hanging starts and 37 of 40 starts near ±90°, over 60-second tests at gravity 1000. It uses a bounded velocity servo and no upright helpers. The same checkpoint still fails at some intermediate angles.

The double pendulum asks a stricter control question: direct acceleration, without a target-velocity servo or upright assistance. A six-ReLU controller optimized with CMA-ES passed 40 of 40 fresh 90-second trials near the standard (55°, 38.5°) release at gravity 850. Both rods stayed above horizontal, with no rail contact. Its wider ±600-pixel track and linked release geometry are part of the result; independently placing both rods near 55° lies outside its reliable range.

Full NEAT continuation now recovers from the linked 42° release at gravity 850 on a wider ±600-pixel track. The earlier policy passed zero of the same 40 fresh starts; the evolved policy passed all 40 at each of three physics resolutions. Its topology changed from 10 to 11 hidden nodes and from 66 to 51 enabled edges. Independent local holds also passed repeated impulse-40 nudges. This is measured high-gravity recovery, not a below-horizontal swing-up.

PPO learns from actual simulator trajectories and backpropagates through the actor and value objectives, without needing physics derivatives. Its frozen double holder also catches both rods from below horizontal when given consistent inward angular velocities. All 80 fresh 90-second starts without extra pushes passed at each of three physics resolutions on the original rail. The interface calls this momentum-assisted swing-up: the supplied initial kinetic energy is essential, and this is not swing-up from rest. Replay enables optional random tip impulses after the first catch, making later recovery an explicitly disturbed experiment. Policy/value loss, gradients, KL and exploration remain visible during fresh PPO training.

sections.heading: Make the difficulty itself inspectable
paragraphs: A triple-pendulum student learned from a local LQR teacher derived from the actual point-mass simulation. Full NEAT then changed its weights and grew the topology from 16 to 17 ReLU hidden nodes. At gravity 1000, with direct acceleration and the original track, the frozen generation-180 policy survived all 40 fresh one-minute impulse-16 sequences at each of three physics resolutions. Every link remained above horizontal without rail contact. The original student failed the same stronger-nudge comparison. The teacher is not called during neural playback; the initialization and subsequent evolution are both explicit.

The Control tab instruments each actual link, phase space, rail use, command saturation, observation clipping and neural activity. Plots now follow display frames while measurements retain every physical step, including brief failures. Its curriculum trace separates displayed-rollout evidence from population or held-out results. A controlled probe keeps the network frozen while testing release angles, finer physics, stronger acceleration, nudges and zero control.

A larger acceleration audit covered six saved double-pendulum neural policies, including legacy entries. Doubling acceleration produced 20/20 NEAT catches from both rods at 140° at 120 Hz, but only 2/20 and 0/20 at finer physics steps in the original audit; all successful runs touched the rail. Every network retained 20/20 recorded-release holds without rail contact at all three resolutions. The NEAT and PPO high-acceleration cases are now playable as explicitly labelled 120 Hz experiments. Each demo shows its recorded physics rate; temporary overrides preserve controller cadence, identify departures from the recorded settings and expose numerical sensitivity directly.

Finite differences of the production simulation show full local controllability rank near upright, while the old triple observations hide an independent velocity direction. Signed angular-rate inputs repair that local information loss. These measurements guide the next experiment; they do not prove global swing-up is reachable. An early neural refinement passed nominal tests but failed finer-step checks, making numerical sensitivity part of the visible engineering evidence.

A same-plant trajectory teacher found nominal large-angle swing-up, but its result changed under physics refinement. A neural student fitted its actions closely yet failed all six autonomous catch tests; teacher-initialized PPO also failed the sustained catch despite rising above-horizontal occupancy. The study exposes these failures to distinguish a good regression fit, a high reward and a robust controller.

sections.heading: Make the reference solution part of the experiment
paragraphs: Both Fourier mechanisms have fixed arm lengths derived from the complete target curve. The analytical version supplies harmonic speeds and initial phases; the CMA-ES controller chooses variable angular velocities from arm state, current tip-to-target error and a loop-phase clock. It trains repeatedly on that curve, without reading the full curve array at each decision. This is learned tracking of known geometry, not learning the Fourier decomposition or generalizing to unseen curves.

The single-pendulum reference pumps energy into the swing and hands control to local LQR. Double and triple references use nonlinear trajectory optimization with time-varying feedback, then local LQR. They integrate their live rigid-body state, accept physical disturbances and passed fresh nudge and timestep-refinement checks. Their driven-pivot equations are explicitly distinct from the neural examples’ point-mass constraint model. Each reference defaults to swing-up followed by nudges; local hold is one toggle away.

A compact controller strip names what is running, whether its behavior is learned, and its current phase. Measured catch-time ranges are in simulation seconds and apply only to the recorded setup without extra manual pushes. These are empirical ranges, not countdowns or guarantees; an observed catch still permits motion. An idle arcade preview shuffles working frozen models and labelled references; the first click, key or scroll hands over control. It pauses when hidden, respects reduced motion and never starts training.

sections.heading: Give each learned mechanism a visible task
paragraphs: Balancing, writing, putting and dodging make a policy's choices easy to relate to. I am interested in the awkward solutions too: an imperfect learned motion can suggest expressive character movement or a game mechanic worth exploring.

A two-link signing mechanism coordinates a cart, rotary servo and telescoping links along a 200-pixel-radius swash. The saved CMA-ES network averages 15.7 pixels of tracking error after a full warm-up period across ten nearby starts, against 122.7 for zero commands. It observes upcoming targets, but receives no analytical motor trajectory. Its shrinking reward tolerance reached 60 pixels; a matched fixed-tolerance run performed nearly as well.

The English-word experiment now trains acquisition explicitly. A small CMA-ES controller learns cart and telescope feedback from neutral commands while the physical joint servo holds its rest bend. All 40 unseen nearby starts kept every complete word below 20 pixels mean pen error: 12.4 pixels on the first loop, 8.3 thereafter. A matched two-seed comparison tested fixed and shrinking tolerance with identical budgets; both worked, so the large improvement cannot be attributed to curriculum alone. The first B retains an approach stroke and numerical sensitivity remains at 480 Hz. Known future-target cues, the approximate ink and the exact spring/servo scene are explicit.

A learned golf swing clears two movable obstacle balls and traverses two fixed domes, then leaves the struck ball to passive physics. It sank all 128 held-out shots within the tested hole and tilt range. The controller is calibrated to this course: it observes ball and hole state, not an arbitrary obstacle map. A compact terrain starter reads local tiles and times jumps, finishing 125 of 128 unseen easy courses. Removing tile observations reduced that to four.

The harder golf course adds two ridges, a movable bumper and a low rebound beam. Contact with the beam is legal. Correcting separating-contact impulses and conditioning saturated neural weights let CMA-ES refine the same course into 200/200 fresh sinks at native 120 Hz and 199/200, 197/200 and 200/200 at 240, 480 and 960 Hz with fixed-rate commands. One club strike launches the ball; later motion is passive. The known layout and tested hole range remain part of the result, rather than a claim of arbitrary-course golf.

A 416-parameter CNN now drives the hard terrain generator. Two local solid/hazard planes pass through four learned convolution filters and max-pooling, then join six body scalars in a dense controller. Separable CMA-ES learned all parameters; the frozen policy completed 72 of 80 untouched hard courses. Untrained, zero-command and raster-masked controls completed none. The live Perception circuit exposes every input plane, filter map, pooled map, body channel and action request. The occupancy sensor and grounded jump-impulse rule are explicit; eight test failures remain.

sections.heading: Measure the behavior that the score is supposed to represent
paragraphs: The model bank retains the learned moving-hole putter and original dense/CNN dodge policies as comparisons. A new CMA-ES-trained scorer ranks nine supplied physical forecasts: 33/40 fresh twenty-second mixed-attack trials at spawn-rate setting 3 survived, with 0.010 registered hits/s in continuous tests. The existing CNN and dense actors survived 0/40 and registered 0.300 and 0.259 hits/s; the hand-designed planner survived 40/40. The physical lookahead is supplied, while its scoring weights are learned. These are comparisons of available checkpoints, not equal-compute architecture rankings.

Removing bullet velocity from the new forecast drops survival to 0/40; restricting it to the nearest eight bullets leaves 33/40 at this density. Motion information is the supported finding. The right panel exposes real scores, forecasts and historical board frames; the history is diagnostic, not a claimed temporal-network input. The explanation separates a temporal CNN, which must learn motion features from images, from a compact scorer supplied with velocity and nine model forecasts. A temporal CNN trained with matched resources remains an untested comparison.

Engineering checks cover mechanics, replay timing, serialization and observation semantics. Signed angular-rate inputs preserve rotation direction when a pendulum link becomes horizontal. The double recovery checkpoint also passed finer-step physics checks with the same control rate. Saved records preserve the complete scene, observation layout and weights; replay outcomes count actual sinks, course completion or sustained holds. The phase-space CNN balancer and differentiable lab remain supporting studies.

The spatial-dodge proof of concept restores two grid-shaped input arrays and a NEAT graph with 548 inputs, three hidden neurons and 2,744 evolved links. It survived 4 of 40 moderate-density twenty-second trials. Removing nearest-bullet state hurt far more than removing images. The varied input display does not imply convolution or strong reliance on the images. Node labels lift above the links on nearby hover; Concise and Loose spacing preserve an inspectable diagram, while glass and embers decorate actual live values. The perception and forecast panels repaint alongside the main viewport. Optional display smoothing eases intensities and bar lengths while numerical values, discrete decisions, timestamped history and physics stay exact.

limitations: Saved model scores apply to the documented scene, start states, hole range, and evaluation duration. Training can converge to a much poorer policy on another seed.
These compact 2D environments are not general robotics benchmarks. Position-based chains, rigid equations, and the dodge game use different dynamics.

The neural triple example uses LQR-teacher initialization followed by NEAT refinement. It is validated for local 1–4° releases and bounded nudges, not random-start learning or swing-up. Larger impulse-20 disturbances remain unreliable.

NEAT and CMA-ES double recovery use wider rails and documented release envelopes. The PPO example starts below horizontal with supplied momentum on the original rail. Reliable learned swing-up from rest at the requested 140° / gravity 850 remains open in this implementation.

The harder golf course is sensitive to contact resolution and is presented as an experiment. A successful catch, lower tracking error, reduced collision count and indefinite reliable control are distinct claims.

kicker: Real-time ray tracer: advanced phenomena & camera internals.

sections.heading: Make the camera part of the renderer
paragraphs: Aperture brings camera geometry, light transport, and computational imaging into one interactive WebGL path tracer. Its tilt-shift showcase lets the user place a plane of focus in the scene and see how that choice changes the rendered depth of field.

The camera samples points across a finite aperture and sends rays toward a focus point. Accumulating those samples produces sharp detail where the rays converge and blur elsewhere. Focal length, aperture size, and focus geometry therefore affect ray generation itself.

sections.heading: A plane of focus, defined by three points
paragraphs: The newer tilt-shift mode adapts Andrew Kensler’s thin-lens construction from Ray Tracing Gems II, Chapter 31. Lens tilt makes an oblique plane of focus possible; the interactive contribution here is connecting that geometry to a directly manipulated three-point gizmo and a progressively rendered scene.

For points A, B, and C, the shader constructs the plane normal n = normalize((B − A) × (C − A)). It transforms the points into camera space to derive a tilted lens basis, samples that lens, and intersects the viewing ray with the chosen focal plane to obtain the ray’s focus target.

This makes a useful rendering problem visible: changing the camera’s sampling geometry changes which parts of a three-dimensional scene appear sharp. The page’s tilt-shift screenshot shows the effect; the demo lets the viewer move the focus plane and inspect it from a new configuration.

links.label: Andrew Kensler — Tilt-Shift Rendering Using a Thin Lens Model

sections.heading: Try the tilt-shift showcase
paragraphs: Use the Thin Lens camera and enable Physically Based Tilt-Shift in the highlighted control group. Enable Show Focal Plane Gizmo for Interactive Control, then lower the F-stop to make changes in depth of field easier to see.
bullets: Drag the colored spheres to rotate the focus plane. Drag the triangle’s center with the left mouse button to translate it parallel to the image plane, or the right button to move it in the perpendicular plane.
Move the plane across objects at different depths and let the progressive image settle after each change. Compare the sharp region with the plane’s position.
Keep the older Film Tilt X/Y controls at zero when exploring the three-point mode: that earlier branch takes precedence when film tilt is active.

sections.heading: Beyond a photographic camera
paragraphs: The same application also exposes wavelength-dependent dispersion, time-of-flight experiments, and holographic capture and reconstruction controls. These make the project a broader computational-optics workbench: the image can represent a measurement that is processed further to recover information about the scene.

The interface separates post-process lens color shifts from its spectral ray-level option. That distinction matters when reading a result: similar-looking color fringes can come from different models. The related time-of-flight essay develops the transient-rendering ideas in more detail.

links.label: Read the time-of-flight rendering deep dive

limitations: The camera is a thin-lens approximation. The three-point branch uses a simplified focal-plane intersection with fallbacks for nearly parallel, behind-camera, or very distant intersections; extreme configurations can produce artifacts.
The newer tilted-lens branch samples a circular disk. The general camera’s other aperture shapes and the older film-tilt approximation should not be read as validated combinations with this mode.

title: Inverse Mechanics & Optics
kicker: Choose the ending. Search for the motion that reaches it.
summary: Place the bodies, choose their destinations, then search for the kicks that get them there—with adjustable preferences for tumbling, impacts or detours through the scene. A C++/WASM simulator makes each candidate testable and replayable. The optical bench asks the same inverse question of caustics, shadows and thread art.

launchers.label: Open mechanics & optics
launchers.description: Choose Inverse Mechanics for contact trajectories or Inverse Caustic for freeform lens design.

sections.heading: Search through contact, then replay the result
paragraphs: A simulation normally tells you what happens next. Here the ending is part of the input: reach these poses, perhaps after tumbling or colliding along the way. It is a small, playable study of an unusual animation tool—directing simulated motion through goals rather than keyframing every event.

The trajectory planner searches release time, push direction, force, and application point, including sequences of pushes. Every candidate runs through the same C++ rigid-body kernel used to execute the chosen shot.

Moving obstacles, compound bodies, friction, and secondary collisions make the objective discontinuous. State restoration and deterministic replay connect the predicted path to the result the visitor can actually fire.

This sits alongside a research direction I find fascinating: controlling simulated animation by searching and browsing possible motions. Twigg and James’s Many-Worlds Browsing is a useful reference for that direction; this workbench uses its own bounded trajectory search, not a reproduction of their system.

sections.heading: A native simulation core with a browser interface
paragraphs: The C++ core holds bodies, contacts, joints, and export buffers in bounded contiguous storage. JavaScript reads typed views of WASM memory for rendering and diagnostics, keeping the boundary explicit.

The solver comparisons expose the behavior of ordered constraints and contact dependencies. They are useful examples of choosing a computation model from the workload rather than treating every simulation step as an interchangeable GPU task.

sections.heading: The same inverse question, asked of light
paragraphs: A freeform lens height field is optimized to form a target caustic. Other chapters solve shadow arrangements and thread density; an anamorphic string construction uses peg height as an additional viewing-dependent image channel.

The optical bench exposes Snell refraction, total internal reflection, Fresnel terms, and irradiance. These are separate forward models with separate design variables, making their capabilities and restrictions inspectable.

limitations: Mechanics searches a bounded control space and can miss a feasible solution; it is not a global reachability guarantee.
The optical bench is a 2.5D study with a restricted parameterization; arbitrary target patterns may be unreachable.

Fast contact remains a discrete approximation: optional adaptive substeps and box-only speculative CCD reduce tunnelling, but do not guarantee swept collision handling for all shapes. The new objective presets enable these safeguards.

sections.heading: The difficult part happens between the diagrams
paragraphs: I usually try to make an algorithm understandable with as little visual machinery as possible. Fortune’s Loom takes a deliberately denser route: the main viewport stays direct and interactive, while the beachline, event queue, tree mutations and numerical decisions remain visible beside it. The beauty is in seeing these parts agree as the construction unfolds.

A finished Voronoi diagram hides most of the engineering that produced it. During Fortune's sweep, arcs split and disappear, neighboring arcs acquire new relationships, scheduled circle events become invalid, and a balanced tree must preserve the same spatial order throughout. Nearly coincident events make those structural decisions depend on numerical comparisons.

Fortune’s Loom lets you inspect those transitions. Geometry, event queues, tree mutations and predicate explanations share a recorded execution. The central question is whether they remain consistent as the input approaches a degenerate configuration—and what evidence identifies the first disagreement.

sections.heading: Six backends, one geometric obligation
paragraphs: The leaf-only AVL beachline stores arcs at leaves and breakpoints at internal nodes. A second representation stores an arc at every node, with AVL, red-black, treap, splay and size-balanced policies. These are six implementations of the same beachline role, with different insertion, removal and rebalancing behavior.

Each tree also maintains threaded neighbors for local event updates. Validation checks that the tree's in-order traversal agrees with that linked order; balancing checks depend on the selected policy. Mutation snapshots expose splits, removals and rotations, including transient states before rebalancing. Agreement across backends supplies differential evidence, while a failed invariant points to a concrete structural operation.

sections.heading: Compare the construction with its reference
paragraphs: Regular rings, grids and nearly coincident events are deliberate test inputs. The A/B view can remove individual robustness measures and compare their consequences: grouped circle collapses, consistent event ordering, geometric disambiguation and stable event storage. The result is a controlled failure case with an inspectable cause.

The raw sweep edges are kept separate from the independently clipped final diagram. Reference-final mode can display repaired geometry, so that polished result alone is not evidence that the sweep succeeded. Raw/reference divergence and regression cases provide the more useful comparison. In the regular 12-site circle, the lowest site arrives at the same geometric time as several cocircular collapses; native and WebAssembly runs can still leave a missing or misplaced spoke. The project records this limit rather than treating every completed image as a correctness certificate.

sections.heading: Show the decision behind the number
paragraphs: Formula-preserving constructions keep an expression graph for quantities such as breakpoints and circle events. Filtered comparisons expose their tolerance intervals, unresolved cases and numerical evaluation. A deliberately reduced-precision mode makes sensitive configurations easier to encounter and compare.

This is an arithmetic audit, not a claim of certified exact computation. The implementation's lazy-exact label does not provide arbitrary precision, exact constructions or symbolic event ordering; the available long-double precision is platform-dependent, and unresolved Apollonius predicates can fall back to the double sign. The regular-circle nadir tie can therefore remain wrong even in that mode. The useful result is visibility into the decision and its uncertainty.

sections.heading: Weighted geometry changes the problem
paragraphs: The Apollonius investigation replaces distance to a point with distance to a disk boundary. Dominated sites can have no cell and bisectors can be curved. Analytic pairwise information is cached incrementally, while topology updates globally reassemble the DCEL. These construction choices and their predicate diagnostics extend the project's core question beyond ordinary point-site Fortune diagrams.

This remains an incomplete implementation of the general paper-based construction. The supported cases and numerical fallbacks are part of the experiment's scope. It should be read as a second, more demanding investigation rather than a completed general-purpose weighted-Voronoi library.

sections.heading: The full construction and the implemented experiment
paragraphs: The reference algorithm maintains an Apollonius graph through specialized conflict predicates and topological updates. This workbench explores the same geometry with a smaller implementation: it can produce and inspect useful weighted diagrams, but some visibility and topology stages remain sampled or incomplete. The distinction is correctness and scope as well as efficiency; the brochure details each boundary.

sections.heading: What changes when the beachline becomes a surface?
paragraphs: The 3D exploration samples a lower envelope of paraboloids, exposing changing patches, adjacency and traces where several owners meet. The sampled grid and estimated events let you explore the higher-dimensional idea, but do not supply a complete solver.

A priority queue can still order event heights. What disappears is the simple left-to-right order of a one-dimensional beachline: a full solver needs robust surface topology, event prediction and local updates. This exploration visualizes that difficulty rather than claiming a completed 3D Fortune algorithm.

limitations: The visualizer records execution snapshots for playback; its frame rate is not an algorithm-throughput benchmark.
Filtered and formula-preserving arithmetic does not constitute certified exact predicates, constructions or event ordering. The weighted-diagram implementation remains incomplete.

Lazy Exact is available in WebAssembly. It retains formulas and refines selected comparisons, but does not certify exact constructions or event ordering. The regular 12-site cocircular case can fail in both native and browser runs.
The dense interface deliberately prioritizes a complete view of the algorithm. Dedicated visualizers elsewhere in the portfolio trade that generality for a more focused presentation.

The browser is a selected C++/WebAssembly port, not a desktop-parity guarantee. Arithmetic representations and enabled features differ by target; difficult inputs must be checked separately. The known cocircular failure is shared by both targets, not evidence of missing browser precision alone.

The C++ project expands that investigation with multiple balance policies, recorded mutations, explicit comparisons and a wider study library. The earlier essay is preserved as an archive. Its broad correctness claims are superseded by the current raw/reference evidence and documented numerical limitations.

sections.heading: The hard part is deciding what a result means
paragraphs: A mathematical expression is both a program to evaluate and a structure to transform. This project investigates the boundary between those roles: how representation exposes an integration method, how a numerical coefficient changes an algebraic decision, and what evidence justifies accepting an answer.

The interface makes those decisions inspectable. Expressions retain their tree structure; transformations carry steps; integration reports its strategy and a verification outcome. The substantial work sits in the engine: canonical forms, polynomial algorithms, a bounded search through integration strategies, and distinct arithmetic domains.

sections.heading: Representation makes a strategy possible
paragraphs: Raw syntax hides useful equivalences. A normalization pass exposes products, powers, and polynomial structure before the integration cascade runs. Sparse polynomial conversion supports long division, GCD cancellation, rational decomposition, and systematic term collection. This reduces dependence on a particular input spelling.

Integration is an ordered heuristic cascade gated by structural tests. Substitution candidates are differentiated and checked for the required proportional factor; rational functions take an algebraic route; other forms reach identities, tables, special functions, or recursive strategies. An unresolved integral remains explicit. The internal ExperimentalRisch name is historical: this is not a complete Risch decision procedure.

sections.heading: Change the domain, change the available solution
paragraphs: Residue integration is a particularly clear example of algorithm selection. A real integral can become a contour problem: supported rational integrands use poles in a selected half-plane, while suitable full-period trigonometric integrals use the unit-circle substitution. The engine reports contour choice, poles, residues, and steps.

The conditions are part of the method. Decay, poles on the path, repeated roots, and the distinction between an improper integral and a principal value all affect what can be concluded. The implementation has a bounded supported family and numerical root/residue calculations; the contour theorem does not make every floating-point output exact.

sections.heading: An arithmetic choice can change the algebraic answer
paragraphs: The exact-arithmetic mode computes with rational coefficients and polynomial algorithms, including GCD, squarefree decomposition, and resultants. Algebraic extensions represent an element as a polynomial in a generator, reduced modulo its defining polynomial; inversion uses extended Euclid. Unsupported exact expressions are refused rather than silently converted to floats.

This matters because a zero test controls structure. Losing a repeated factor changes a polynomial GCD, not just the last decimal place. The comparison between floating point, interval enclosures, and exact arithmetic makes the consequence visible. Interval and exact tools have separate supported domains; neither upgrades the whole engine into a certified CAS.

sections.heading: Make the evidence travel with the answer
paragraphs: The integration check differentiates a candidate antiderivative and compares it with the input at sampled points. Both desktop and browser interfaces show that check alongside the formula. A partial result has no completed-antiderivative verdict.

Sample agreement is useful evidence, not an identity proof or a probability of correctness. This distinction is essential when numerical roots, branch choices, singularities, or an unfamiliar input can invalidate a plausible answer. Regression probes cover parser precedence, simplifier termination, improper-integral rejection, residue cases, and the verdict crossing the application boundary.

sections.heading: One engine, two execution environments
paragraphs: The desktop route uses Sinatra. The static route packages the same Ruby modules in dependency order and evaluates that bundle in CRuby through ruby.wasm. A browser adapter maps the existing API-shaped calls into the local VM; the symbolic algorithms are not reimplemented in JavaScript.

The browser downloads the Ruby interpreter and interface dependencies, then computes locally. Startup takes time, and a long symbolic calculation can block the interface. Additional tools such as moving-domain calculus, Padé approximation, field operators, and equation discovery are secondary investigations built around the same expression infrastructure.

limitations: The integration cascade is heuristic and incomplete; supported transformations do not amount to a general Risch implementation.
Numerical spot-checks are evidence, not formal proofs. Sample agreement percentages must not be read as calibrated confidence.
Exact rational/algebraic tools, interval methods, numerical residue evaluation, and ordinary symbolic transforms have different domains and guarantees.
The static build requires browser WebAssembly and external runtime downloads. Long synchronous Ruby calculations can block the page.

sections.heading: What if the captured light becomes the scene?
paragraphs: A camera image records how a scene looks along many directions from one position. Arrange calibrated cameras in space and the collection becomes a sampled light field. LightField / Neural makes that representation tangible: each captured position acts as a virtual directional source, and a freely moving viewer constructs an image from the stored ray samples.

The geometric picture is useful on its own. Moving between the sample points changes the available directions; widening the matching kernel joins their contributions; changing focus aligns different depths. The viewer reconstructs appearance from recorded images without requiring a learned scene model. Its virtual sources supply directional image values to the renderer; they are not new point lights used to illuminate scene geometry.

Faithful reconstruction is one aim; the surreal behavior between observations is another. Like the photon-primitive studies, this work also asks what the representation makes visually interesting when its approximation becomes visible.

sections.heading: Render and reshape the sampled ray field
paragraphs: The 3D ray-space view combines calibrated positions, look directions and image samples. For each virtual-camera ray, the renderer selects eligible captured views, projects into their directional images and combines their colors. Camera markers, the scene map and coverage views keep those decisions connected to visible geometry.

Sharp and Smooth ray matching expose the effect of interpolation width. Refocus uses a chosen focal plane and the camera array as aperture samples, so aligned features remain sharper while other depths spread across the combined image. A projection sweep supplies a separate exploratory blend through multiple proxy depths. These are directly rendered views of the captured field.

Epipolar slices connect a fixed image row across camera positions, and patch matching provides a normalized disparity display. Interpolation assumptions remain visible in disocclusions, layer blending and sparse-view artifacts; the disparity display is not calibrated metric depth for every rig.

New recording presets contrast a dense 432-view orbit with a 36-view control and a separate 441-view planar refocus array. Lower-resolution captures make the distinction between directional coverage, view density and synthetic aperture easier to explore.

sections.heading: From explicit light samples to learned appearance
paragraphs: NeRF and Gaussian splatting offer two further ways to render the observed scene. The light field keeps images and calibrated sample positions explicit; NeRF stores density and directional color in neural functions; Gaussian splatting stores projected spatial primitives. The native application connects Python training, checkpoints and previews to the same inspection workspace, with project implementations and reference integrations identified.

The supplied Cornell capture includes 56 training cameras and eight test cameras. Existing artifacts contain completed NeRF and reference-GS runs with test-view renders, allowing visible differences to be examined now. Their settings and budgets differ, so the images demonstrate the pipeline and its present reconstruction quality rather than establishing which method is universally better. The wider method registry remains exploratory.

sections.heading: Match the view before interpreting the difference
paragraphs: A shared inspection camera connects direct light-field synthesis, supported Gaussian / NeRF / Instant-NGP checkpoints and a path-traced source reference. Saved test-camera outputs support matched comparisons; free-camera exploration reveals coverage gaps. Method, training budget and permitted input views still need to match before treating a visual difference as a benchmark.

The generic evaluation path now requires an explicit manifest pairing each rendered image with its reference camera. Filenames alone cannot establish correspondence because the capture, NeRF and Gaussian exporters use different numbering conventions. An unavailable perceptual metric remains unavailable in the report rather than becoming a misleading zero.

The next useful experiment is a controlled change in camera coverage: hold the scene, representation, training budget, and test poses fixed, then vary the acquisition rig. Compare errors on visible surfaces, disocclusions, and empty regions separately. That gives image quality a cause and turns the workbench into a study of what the measurements can support.

title: Inverse Render Lab
kicker: Reconstructing shapes from renders—and seeing around corners.
summary: Three connected inverse problems: reconstruct a 3D shape, separate material from illumination, and image around a corner. Inspect the measurements, solver, and residual to see what each reconstruction actually establishes.
